forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change: Down 1pp to 23%. Quiet Sunday news cycle, no fresh AGI declaration. The Information / SaaStr coverage this week confirms OpenAI's AGI clause has been swapped for granular capability gates in the renegotiated Microsoft deal, structurally de-emphasising binary AGI framing. GPT-5.5 (released early May) and Anthropic Mythos Preview both posting strong cyber/agentic gains but framed as capability milestones, not AGI. With ~31 months left and no lab declaration in the pipeline, modest downward drift.
forecasts.base_rate: ~20-24% aggregated from Metaculus (~31% on weakly-general AI by 2030), Kalshi (~38% OpenAI-specific by 2030), and superforecaster surveys
factors_up: Anthropic Mythos Preview cleared UK AISI 32-step cyber range (3/10 runs); GPT-5.5 cleared it three weeks later (+2pp)
Anthropic '2028 Two Scenarios' paper still publicly anchors leadership AGI timeline (+1pp)
Compute scale: Anthropic $200B commitment + Colossus 1 (220k Nvidia) access (+1pp)
factors_down: OpenAI-Microsoft contract drops AGI clause for capability gates — structural shift away from binary AGI framing (-2pp)
Resolution requires explicit lab declaration or 3+ researcher endorsement — high evidentiary bar (-2pp)
WhatLLM.org May summary characterises the month as 'the frontier took a breath' — architecture pivot rather than capability leap (-1pp)
Time decay: ~31 months remaining; quiet Sunday with no headline shifts (-1pp)
key_uncertainties: Whether the Microsoft AGI clause change reflects internal pessimism or pure contractual hygiene
Whether Anthropic Mythos full release in H2 2026 is framed as AGI
Whether a competitor (xAI, Google DeepMind) makes the first declaration to seize narrative

update_triggers.up: Public AGI declaration from any frontier lab; Mythos full release with AGI framing; coordinated 3+ researcher endorsement
update_triggers.down: Capability plateau on next-gen benchmarks; further contract language stripping AGI references; CAISI/regulatory pre-disclosure delay

forecasts.question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 25%. CaseInterviewHub crisis piece consolidates the picture: McKinsey 200 tech/support cuts late 2025 plus signalled ~10% non-client reduction over two years; Bain, Deloitte, KPMG, Accenture all trimmed in 2025; PwC and EY deferred start dates. BCG is the outlier (growing on AI/tech specialist hires). Pattern is back-office automation and demand softness, not yet a revenue cliff. 65% of enterprises citing traditional consulting as insufficient value adds longer-term risk. Trajectory consistent with prior tracking.
forecasts.base_rate: ~10-15% base rate for ≥33% industry contractions over a 6-year horizon (historical decadal shocks: legal post-2008, advertising agencies post-2010)
factors_up: McKinsey 10% non-client-facing reduction signalled across two years confirms structural, not cyclical, cuts (+3pp)
150k+ tech/corporate role eliminations globally YTD 2026, consulting in top tier (+2pp)
65% of enterprises now say traditional consulting models don't provide enough value (+2pp)
~25% of entry-level consulting/finance postings now require AI skills — entry-level pyramid eroding (+2pp)
factors_down: Cuts concentrated in back-office, not client-facing revenue — revenue resilience persists (-3pp)
BCG outlier growing headcount on AI/tech specialists suggests substitution, not pure displacement (-2pp)
33% threshold is severe; 6-year horizon allows industry to pivot to AI-augmented model (-3pp)
Big 4 advisory still posting growth; only management consulting segment under pressure (-2pp)
key_uncertainties: Whether 2026 Q2/Q3 revenue prints from MBB show absolute declines vs flat
Whether AI implementation work absorbs displaced consultants or is captured by tech vendors
How '2+ credible analyses primarily attributing to AI' resolution criterion will be judged

update_triggers.up: MBB firm announces double-digit revenue decline; 20%+ headcount cut announced at any tier-1 firm; major client publicly cancels engagement citing AI
update_triggers.down: MBB Q3 revenue beat; AI implementation engagements drive net headcount growth; sector returns to 2023 trend

forecasts.question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 3%. Latest YouGov (4-5 May): Reform 25%, Labour 18%, Conservatives 17%, Greens 15%, Lib Dems 14%. PollCheck 7-poll moving average (13 May): Reform 28.1%, Labour 18.9%, Conservatives 19.0%. Labour now within margin of error of Conservatives in some trackers and trailing Reform by 7-10pp. With election deadline by Dec 2029 (~3.5 years out), Labour would need a sustained 7-10pp swing to overtake Reform. No reversal signal in the data.
forecasts.base_rate: ~8-12% base rate for governing parties trailing by 7-10pp at this stage to recover and win most seats (historical UK precedents: 1992 Major recovery being a partial counterexample)
factors_up: FPTP can deliver largest party with ~30% if vote splits favourably across Reform/Con/Green (+2pp)
~3.5 years to election allows time for incumbency recovery (+2pp)
Reform vote may not turn out at GE turnout levels (+1pp)
factors_down: Labour at 18% in latest YouGov, below the 24-26% it polled in equivalent Conservative-led 2010-2015 cycle (-3pp)
Reform leading consistently at 25-28% in polls and moving-averages (-3pp)
5-way fragmentation reduces Labour's FPTP geographic efficiency advantage (-2pp)
Greens at 14-15% eat into Labour's progressive vote share (-2pp)
MRP modelling of 2026 London locals shows close races — even Labour's traditional strongholds contested (-1pp)
key_uncertainties: Whether Reform vote holds through to GE turnout
Whether Labour leadership change before 2029 prompts a poll bounce
Whether tactical voting emerges to coordinate anti-Reform vote

update_triggers.up: Labour overtakes Reform in 3+ polls; Reform faces leadership crisis; tactical voting pact emerges
update_triggers.down: Reform extends lead beyond 30%; Labour conference produces no rebound; by-election losses to Reform in Labour heartlands

factors_up: Sustained PLA mapping/prep work in Bashi Channel — operational readiness improving (+1pp)
Bomber+missile demonstrations during multilateral exercise signal coercive intent (+1pp)
Xi's stated 2027 PLA readiness target remains in window (+1pp)
factors_down: PLA actions remain reactive/scripted (responding to Balikatan), not initiative-taking (-2pp)
US-China strategic stability framework (post-Beijing summit) may dampen escalation appetite (-1pp)
Economic costs of blockade prohibitive given PRC growth pressures (-2pp)
Taiwan 2028 election cycle creates political incentive to delay escalation (-1pp)
No mobilisation indicators in OSINT (rail/shipping/medical) (-1pp)
key_uncertainties: Whether PLA 2027 readiness translates to action or remains contingency planning
How US deterrent posture evolves under Trump administration through 2028
Whether a Taiwan political crisis (e.g. unilateral declaration) triggers PRC action

forecasts.question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 1%. ONS March 2026 release (22 April) showed CPI 12-month rate 3.3%, UP from 3.0% in February — rise driven by transport costs and motor fuels reflecting Middle East energy price spike. Core inflation 3.1%, services inflation 4.5% (up from 4.3%). April 2026 release published but specific figure not yet circulated in trackers. With only 8 monthly prints remaining before Jan 2027 deadline and inflation moving in the wrong direction, the path to sub-2% requires a 1.3pp+ drop in 7-8 months — unprecedented absent recession or energy shock reversal.
forecasts.base_rate: <2% historical frequency of 1.3pp+ CPI drops in 8 months absent recession or major commodity reversal
factors_up: Base effects: high prints from late 2025 roll off in late 2026 (+1pp)
Possible Middle East ceasefire could rapidly reverse energy spike (+1pp)
factors_down: March 2026 CPI rose to 3.3% — moving in wrong direction (-2pp)
Services inflation 4.5% is sticky and dominant driver (-2pp)
BoE April MPR signals inflation persistence (-1pp)
Only 8 monthly prints remain to Jan 2027 deadline (-2pp)
Core 3.1% well above target — wage growth still elevated (-1pp)
key_uncertainties: Pace of Middle East energy price normalisation
Wage settlement round outcomes for 2026/27 pay year
Whether the 2026 fiscal stance becomes restrictive enough to disinflate services

update_triggers.up: Single CPI print drops by 1pp+ in one month; oil prices fall 30%+; BoE materially cuts inflation forecast
update_triggers.down: April/May 2026 CPI prints above 3.3%; energy prices spike further; services inflation breaks above 5%

forecasts.question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
forecasts.key_change: Down 1pp to 37%. OBR March 2026 EFO confirms underlying TFP growth assumption 0.8% (revised down from 1.1%), with labour supply growth declining to 0.5% by 2030 driven by lower migration and ageing. Implied trend GDP growth ≈1.3% — below the 1.5% threshold. House of Commons Library piece reinforces 'persistently weak productivity remains UK's primary obstacle' and pre-GFC trend gap of ~25%. Public debt at 95% of GDP early 2030s limits fiscal capacity for growth-boosting investment.
forecasts.base_rate: UK 10-year average real GDP growth 2010-2019 was ~2.0%, 2014-2023 was ~1.4%. Trend has slowed; reaching 1.5% across full 2030s requires either AI-driven productivity boom or migration reversal
factors_up: AI productivity diffusion could lift TFP above 0.8% trend (+3pp)
Labour government 1.5m homes commitment + planning reform could boost investment (+2pp)
Base effects from 2030 recovery if 2027-29 stagnation creates a low base (+1pp)
factors_down: OBR underlying TFP assumption 0.8% confirmed in March 2026 EFO — below required pace (-3pp)
Labour supply growth declining to 0.5% by 2030 (-2pp)
Public debt 95% of GDP early 2030s constrains fiscal expansion (-2pp)
Pre-GFC trend gap of ~25% suggests structural drag not yet reversed (-2pp)
Climate/energy transition costs front-loaded into 2030s (-1pp)
key_uncertainties: Whether AI productivity gains materialise broadly rather than narrowly in tech
Whether migration policy reverses or remains restrictive
Resolution measurement methodology (ONS arithmetic mean) — sensitive to single-year recessions

update_triggers.up: OBR revises TFP assumption back to 1%+ in autumn EFO; AI productivity literature consensus shifts upward; major investment shock (sovereign wealth fund, EU rejoin)
update_triggers.down: OBR cuts TFP below 0.8%; recession scenario in 2027-29 baked into projections; migration falls below 200k net
